analysis.one_liner: Charges large cargo ships per ton of emissions and spends it on cleaner ports.
analysis.headline: The bill drew four cosponsors, was referred to five House committees, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require operators of large cargo ships on voyages to or from U.S. ports to report their fuel use and routes, then charge them $150 per metric ton of carbon dioxide-equivalent emissions from their fuel, plus per-pound fees on smog and soot pollutants released in U.S. waters, with the carbon fee tripled for fuel burned in polar regions. Importers who route U.S.-bound cargo through foreign ports would pay a prorated version of the fee. The money would fund battery-electric ferries and harbor craft, cleaner Jones Act ships, low-carbon fuel research, and fenceline air monitoring in communities within a mile of ports.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near ports, who would get fenceline air monitoring and, over time, less ship and port pollution; communities in poor-air-quality areas, which grant programs must prioritize; ferry riders and harbor users; and everyone who shares in the benefit of cutting a shipping industry responsible for roughly 3 percent of global carbon dioxide emissions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Port neighbors and ferry and harbor communities

how_it_helps.text: Fees are charged per ton of lifecycle carbon dioxide-equivalent emissions from cargo-voyage fuel ($150 per metric ton, rising with inflation plus 5 points a year, tripled in polar regions) and per pound of nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide, and fine particulate matter released in U.S. waters.

100 percent of fee collections are recycled into public purposes: 25 percent for replacing or retrofitting dirty Jones Act vessels, 25 percent for low-carbon marine fuel and technology grants, 10 percent each for harbor craft and ferry electrification, 5 percent for maritime workforce training, 3 percent for air monitoring in communities within one mile of a port, 10 percent for the Clean Ports program, 7 percent for port infrastructure, and 3 and 2 percent for oceans security and marine debris programs.
Grant selection must prioritize public health and environmental benefits per dollar and relief for areas in violation of air quality standards or receiving disproportionate pollution.

The bill cites findings that marine shipping accounts for nearly 3 percent of global carbon dioxide emissions and that ports worsen health outcomes in surrounding neighborhoods, and it sunsets automatically if an international body imposes an equal or larger global fee.
Operators that fail to pay can be barred from U.S. waters and ports by the Coast Guard, and importers who do not pay can have their cargo seized at the border, giving the fee real teeth.

analysis.who_pays: Ocean shipping operators and importers bear the fees, and some portion would be passed through to shoppers as modestly higher prices on shipped goods; shippers also face detailed quarterly reporting on fuel, cargo, and routes.

drawbacks.text: The fee is assessed directly on shipping operators and on importers of U.S.-bound cargo, and the costs of such shipping fees are generally passed along, raising prices on imported goods for consumers.

A quarter of the revenue goes to grants for owners of Jones Act vessels, a concentrated group of domestic shipowners, so a share of the money is a subsidy to private companies even as it cleans up their fleets.
The fees and reporting requirements would take effect January 1, 2025 with no phase-in, giving shippers little time to adjust routes, fuel, or billing.
The bill could create friction with trading partners; its relief for foreign fees only applies if the origin country's fee reaches at least half the U.S. fee.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade is a modest, broad cost in the price of shipped goods for a targeted cleanup of one of the world's largest untaxed pollution sources, with the money spent in the neighborhoods that breathe port pollution. The main design weaknesses are the no-phase-in start date and the large share of revenue flowing to private vessel owners, but the fee structure is transparent, escalates over time, and disappears if an international fee takes its place.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to five House committees on the day it was introduced and later to a Trade subcommittee, but no committee ever held a hearing or vote on it, and it never reached the House floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Doris Matsui introduced the bill on July 11, 2024, joined on introduction by Reps. Mullin and Takano.

It was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, Science, Space and Technology, Ways and Means, and Natural Resources Committees, with no action beyond referral in any of them.
On December 17, 2024, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Trade, and no further action followed.
The bill ended the 118th Congress with four cosponsors and no vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: International shipping operators and importers never paid the emissions fees, and the fee-funded port electrification, fuel research, and fenceline air-monitoring programs were never created; port-adjacent communities saw none of the promised monitoring or cleanup.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Shipping operators and importers who avoided the fee

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all four cosponsors were Democrats; Republicans, holding 226 of 442 House seats and the chairs of all five committees of referral, offered no support and the bill never advanced past referral.

industries.note: The bill charges them up to $150 per metric ton of carbon dioxide-equivalent from voyage fuel, per-pound fees on smog and soot pollutants in U.S. waters, a tripled polar rate, and detailed quarterly reporting, with nonpayment punishable by a Coast Guard ban from U.S. ports. Their cost is the air-quality and climate gain the fee is designed to buy.

industries.industry: Importers of foreign-made goods and big-box retailers
industries.note: Importers must report and pay a prorated fee on U.S.-bound cargo routed through foreign ports, on pain of cargo seizure, which raises landed costs they tend to pass to shoppers. Their interest in cheap shipping runs against the cleaner air and emissions reductions the fee funds.

industries.industry: U.S. domestic shipping (Jones Act fleet owners)
industries.note: A quarter of fee collections go to grants, rebates, and loans to replace or retrofit Jones Act vessels with batteries or low-carbon fuels, prioritizing pollution relief in poor-air-quality areas. It is a subsidy to a concentrated group of vessel owners, paid for by the new fees, that also cuts port pollution.

industries.industry: Sustainable marine fuel and low-emission technology producers
industries.note: Another quarter of the collections fund competitive grants for producing, moving, and storing low-carbon maritime fuels and developing low-emission technologies, with job creation an explicit priority. The fee creates both funding and demand for their products.

industries.industry: Port authorities, ferry and harbor craft operators
industries.note: The bill directs 10 percent of collections each to harbor-craft and ferry electrification, 10 percent to the Clean Ports program, 7 percent to port infrastructure, and 5 percent to workforce training. Cleaner equipment and monitoring serve the port neighborhoods that breathe the pollution.
